docs.title: General Questions
docs.text:
Q: What is RECAP? A: RECAP is a hardware adapter that records both sides of a conversation by splitting headset audio into a stereo signal — your voice on one channel, theirs on the other.

Q: Do I need special software? A: Use recording software that selects the connected external input and captures both stereo channels separately. Verify the result with the two-sided test.

Q: What devices work as the CALL source? A: A device with an AHJ/CTIA 3.5mm TRRS headset path is a candidate. A working headset establishes a direct-call baseline, not compatibility of the complete RECAP recording chain. Check the compatibility checklist, including microphone-capable adapters/app routing, then run the two-sided test.

Q: Can I use RECAP with my computer's headset port? A: Yes, as the call device. If your computer has a combo headset jack (common on laptops), RECAP plugs into it and you take Zoom, Teams or other calls through your headset. The recording itself goes to a separate recording device whose input is a stereo microphone input with plug-in power. See the Zoom question below.

Q: Do I need batteries? A: No batteries are required. Use the supported external stereo MIC-mode setup with plug-in power where supported. Earlier explanations that recorder bias powers S2 were not adequately supported; see the correction and pending validation.

docs.title: Compatibility Questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do I only hear one side of the conversation? A: First distinguish one ear in the live headset from a missing recorded channel. A mono recording input is one possibility; wrong input selection, headset/app routing, cabling, gain or processing can also lose a voice. Use recording troubleshooting and the two-sided test; a scanner result alone does not identify the cause.

Q: Why doesn't RECAP work with my Mac? A: Check the actual selected external input against the compatibility checklist. A Mac model name or failed recording does not establish input capability or the cause. If the input is confirmed to lack stereo MIC capture, use a suitable interface; see the adapter guide.

Q: Can I record to my iPhone or Android phone? A: Not directly — mobile devices have combo ports, not stereo MIC IN. However, you can use a USB audio adapter (with stereo mic input) connected to your phone's USB-C or Lightning port. This adds a proper stereo input for RECAP. A plain Lightning or USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter is not enough here. That adapter is the fix for the phone you make calls on, not for the one you record onto.

Q: Will RECAP work with my computer? A: The scanner reports the selected capture path's channel capability. STEREO does not prove the complete chain works, and MONO calls for checking the selected input/mode before choosing an interface. Follow the compatibility checklist and two-sided test.

Q: What's the difference between MIC IN and LINE IN? A: Use an external stereo microphone input with MIC mode and plug-in power where supported. Line-only operation is outside the supported setup; port color alone does not establish input capability. See recorder requirements.

docs.title: Setup Questions
docs.text:
Q: Can I hear the call while recording? A: Yes! Connect your headset to RECAP and you'll hear the call in real-time while it records.

Q: Which headset should I use? A: A wired headset with the microphone on the cable, which means a 4-pole (TRRS) plug with a boom or an inline mic. It also has to work with your phone: plug it straight into the phone and make a call. Apple 3.5mm EarPods work well as a reference. A headset that works with your phone but has no mic on the cable will not record your voice, because your phone uses its own built-in microphone instead. See Headset Compatibility.

Q: Why is my recording very quiet? A: Check the selected external input, recording gain and processing. Raise gain while watching for clipping, then check each participant's recorded channel in the two-sided test. Low level alone does not establish a cause.

docs.title: Recording Questions
docs.text:
Q: Can I record to a voice recorder instead of computer? A: A recorder is a candidate if its external input meets the recorder checklist. Use stereo MIC mode, plug-in power where supported, and processing off for the initial two-sided test. Matching specifications are not a physically tested configuration; electrical validation remains pending. Never connect phantom power.

Q: Can I use RECAP with Zoom, Teams, or Skype calls on my computer? A: A computer can be CALL when its AHJ/CTIA wired headset path carries both app audio and the headset mic. Use a separate REC device meeting the checklist, and confirm routing/capture with the two-sided test. The app name or headset jack alone does not certify the complete chain.

Q: What recording quality should I use? A: For best quality: WAV format, 44.1kHz or 48kHz sample rate, 16-bit depth. For smaller files: MP3 at 192kbps or higher.

Q: Can I record on both sides in separate files? A: Yes, in Audacity. Record in stereo, then use "Split Stereo Track". Each voice lands on its own track. Which one is left and which is right depends on your recording device, so play each track once and label it (see Channel Swap).

docs.title: Troubleshooting Questions
docs.text:
Q: My headset works with my phone but not with RECAP. Why? A: This is rare but can happen with unusual headset wiring. Try a different headset (Apple EarPods are a good test). If multiple headsets fail, contact support.

Q: I hear static or noise. What's wrong? A: Check all connections are firm. Move RECAP away from power adapters. Lower microphone gain to 70-80%. Try a different headset.

Q: Can I use a splitter cable to record to multiple devices? A: No supported configuration for splitters exists.

docs.title: Product Questions
docs.text:
Q: Is RECAP wireless/Bluetooth? A: No. RECAP is a wired hardware adapter. Bluetooth has too much latency for real-time call recording.

Q: Can I use RECAP with a mixer or recording equipment? A: Never use RECAP with +48V phantom power - it is outside the supported setup. For professional equipment, you may need a different interface.

Q: How long does RECAP last? A: RECAP has no batteries or moving parts. With proper care, it should last indefinitely.

docs.title: Technical Questions
docs.text:
Q: What is MONO vs STEREO input? A: STEREO input has 2 channels (can record left and right separately). MONO input has 1 channel (records only one side). RECAP requires STEREO to record both sides of conversation.

Q: What is AHJ standard? A: American Headset Jack - the standard headphone connector pinout used by iPhone, Android, and most cell phones. Opposite of OMTP (rare, older phones).

Q: Why does the scanner show my input as MONO? A: The browser/driver reports one capture channel for the selected input. Confirm that it is the intended physical external input and check stereo/mono mode; brand or age does not establish capability. Use the two-sided test, and consider an interface only if the actual input is confirmed insufficient.

docs.title: What to tell us
docs.text:
You do not need to finish a diagnostic checklist before writing in. But RECAP sits in a chain of three or four devices, and the same symptom can come from any link in it — so these five answers are usually the difference between one reply and five.

1. What device do you make calls on? Phone, desk phone, tablet, or computer — and the model if you have it handy.

2. What are you recording onto? A computer, a voice recorder, a phone with a USB audio adapter — or nothing yet. This is a separate device from the one you make calls on.

3. Does your headset have a microphone on the cable, and what make and model is it? Look for a boom arm, or a small inline blob partway down the wire. This one matters more than any other answer — see Headset Compatibility. The model helps us spot the handful of headsets that are wired unusually.

4. What is plugged into what? The full chain, in order. The easiest way to tell us is against this connection diagram — say where your setup matches it and where it differs. That's far more useful than a description in words.

5. Does it work without RECAP? Plug the headset straight into your call device and make a test call. Can you hear them, and can they hear you?

If it's a recording problem, add: a screenshot of the device scanner results, what you hear on playback (silence, one side only, too quiet), your operating system and recording software, and — if you swapped the cable that came in the box — what cable you're using instead.

If your callers say you sound muffled, add: which rung of the three-rung ladder it first got worse at.

docs.title: What is RECAP?
docs.text:
RECAP is a small hardware adapter that records both sides of any conversation — phone calls, computer meetings, or any audio through a headset.

What it does:

  • Captures both sides of the conversation (your voice + their voice)
  • Works with any device that has a combo headset port (phones, laptops, tablets)
  • Outputs to any device with stereo microphone input
  • Pass-through audio so you can hear in real-time

What you get:

  • One channel: Your voice from the headset mic
  • Other channel: Their voice from the call device
  • ⚠️ Channel assignment (L/R) may vary depending on USB adapter used

What you need: Call device + Headset + Recording device + Recording software (free)

docs.title: Required Items
docs.text:
1. Call device with combo headset port

  • Phone (with 3.5mm jack or Lightning/USB-C adapter)
  • Laptop or computer with combo headset jack
  • Tablet with 3.5mm jack
  • Any device using standard AHJ headset connector

2. Compatible headset

  • ⚠️ CRITICAL: Many old headsets don't work with modern devices
  • Test your headset FIRST (see Step 1 below)
  • Apple EarPods work well as a reference headset

3. Recording device with STEREO microphone input

  • This is where most issues happen
  • Most modern laptops/Macs only have MONO input

  • Use our free scanner to check: https://recapmycalls.com/audio/

  • If MONO only → You need a USB adapter that adds a stereo mic input (which ones)

4. Recording software (free)

  • Windows: Sound Recorder (built-in) or Audacity (recommended)
  • Mac: QuickTime Player (built-in) or Audacity (recommended)
  • Download Audacity: https://www.audacityteam.org

docs.title: Items Included with RECAP
docs.text:
• RECAP S2 device (white adapter)
  • Connection cord (3.5mm audio cable, 1 meter)
  • This user manual

docs.title: Step 1: Test Your Headset (2 minutes)
docs.text:
⚠️ DO NOT SKIP THIS STEP

Many people grab an old headset from a drawer that doesn't work with their phone. Test it FIRST before connecting RECAP.

How to test:

  1. Plug headset directly into your phone (no RECAP)
  2. Make a test call to a friend or voicemail
  3. Check:
  4. ✅ Can you hear them clearly?
  5. ✅ Can they hear you clearly?

Results:

  • ✅ Both YES → The direct-call audio check passed. Confirm the wired headset mic is active using the mic-routing check, then continue to Step 2.
  • ❌ Either NO → Check headset connections, the phone adapter and app routing before adding RECAP; this result alone does not identify which part needs attention.

Why this matters: If your headset doesn't work with your phone directly, RECAP cannot fix it.

"They can hear me, but they say I sound muffled or distant." That usually means there's no microphone on the headset cable, or the adapter isn't carrying the mic channel — see Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant. Sort this out before adding RECAP; RECAP can't improve what the phone is already sending.

docs.title: Step 2: Pass-Through Test (2 minutes)
docs.text:
⚠️ You DON'T need your computer for this test

This checks the headset playback path through RECAP before connecting the separate recording device (REC). The recording channels remain untested.

Make the connections:

Phone ──→ RECAP ──→ Headset

Connection details:

  1. Plug your headset into RECAP's headset jack
  2. Plug RECAP into your phone's headphone jack (or Lightning/USB-C adapter)
  3. Don't connect to computer yet

⚠️ Connection order matters. Always connect the headset to RECAP before plugging RECAP into your phone. When a Lightning or USB-C adapter is plugged in, your phone immediately decides how to route audio. If the headset isn't already in the chain, the phone may not recognize it as a headset setup — causing audio to route to the speaker instead. See Connection Order troubleshooting for details.

Pass-through test:

  1. Make a test call on your phone
  2. Can you hear the call clearly in your headset?

Results:

  • ✅ YES → The headset playback path passed this test. The recording channels remain untested; continue to Step 3.
  • ❌ NO → Compare with the direct-headset baseline in Step 1, then check connections, adapter and app routing. This does not identify a cause; contact support if it remains unresolved.

docs.title: Step 3: Check Computer Compatibility (1 minute)
docs.text:
⚠️ BEFORE plugging RECAP into computer, check compatibility

Run the device scanner:

👉 https://recapmycalls.com/audio/

This free browser tool scans your computer's audio inputs.

What you'll see:

  • "STEREO input detected (2 channels)" → The selected capture path reports two channels. Continue to Step 4 and verify independent two-sided capture; the scan alone does not prove the complete setup works.
  • "MONO input detected (1 channel)" → Check that the intended physical external input and stereo recording mode are selected. A mono capture cannot preserve S2's separate channels.

If the intended input is confirmed to lack stereo MIC capture, use another supported input or a suitable stereo microphone interface. Computer brand/age and scanner channel count alone establish neither a unit defect nor its absence. Follow the compatibility checklist and two-sided test.

Take a screenshot of the scanner results - helpful if you need support later.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect to Computer & Record (2 minutes)
docs.text:
NOW connect to your computer:

Phone ──→ RECAP ──→ Headset
            │
            └──→ Computer MIC IN (or USB Adapter)

Connection:

  • Use included cable to connect RECAP's MIC output to:
  • If STEREO input: Computer's MIC IN port (pink or mic icon)
  • If MONO input: USB adapter's MIC IN jack → USB adapter → Computer USB port

⚠️ Must be MIC IN (not LINE IN)

⚠️ Unplug from the phone first, then rebuild with the phone LAST. Don't add the recording cable to a chain that's already plugged into your phone — that's the connection order problem again. Disconnect from the phone, connect headset → RECAP → recording cable, then plug into the phone last. See Connection Order troubleshooting.

Open recording software:

Windows:

  • Press Windows key, type "sound recorder", press Enter
  • Click "Start Recording" button

Mac:

  • Open QuickTime Player
  • File → New Audio Recording
  • Click dropdown next to record button → Select "External Microphone"
  • Click red record button

Make a two-sided test recording:

Follow the setup and two-sided test, including app routing and a phrase from each participant. Verify both voices at useful levels on separate recorded channels before relying on the setup.

Problems?

  • One-sided or no audio → Go to Troubleshooting
  • Very quiet audio → See "Low Volume" solution

🎉 That's it! You're ready to record calls.

After first-time setup, it's plug-and-play. Just connect everything and hit record.

docs.title: Compatibility checklist
docs.text:
Use a call device (CALL) and a separate recording device (REC). Check the connection and input specifications, rather than a product name or headphone jack alone.

Part What to check CALL phone/device A 3.5 mm AHJ/CTIA TRRS headset connection, directly or through a microphone-capable adapter Phone adapter Correct Lightning/USB-C connector and microphone input support; a headphone-only adapter cannot carry your headset mic Headset Wired 3.5 mm TRRS, 4 contacts / 3 insulating bands, with an inline or boom microphone; it must work on CALL with the same adapter Recording cable Included 3.5 mm male-to-male TRS, 3 contacts / 2 insulating bands, straight-through stereo cable; a TRRS headset cable is a different part REC input External stereo microphone input (two channels); MIC mode where selectable, with plug-in power enabled where supported; no phantom power Recording settings Select the connected external input, record both channels separately, and turn off mono mixing and processing for the initial test Calling app Call audio and the headset microphone must both route through the wired headset path, including in apps such as Teams

Before an important call: follow setup and the two-sided test. For recorder details and the open electrical-validation issue, see Recording Device Compatibility.

docs.title: What a compatibility claim means
docs.text:
A physically tested configuration needs a recorded test for those exact models and settings. A tested phone adapter does not validate every phone, app or recorder used with it. A specification-based expectation means the manufacturer's manual matches the requirements; it is useful evidence, but not certification or a guarantee for the whole chain. If the evidence is missing, compatibility is unresolved.

If our setup instructions are unclear or the documented setup fails, contact support with the specific question or symptom. We can help isolate the RECAP setup; you do not need a full device inventory for a general requirements question.

docs.title: Call Device Compatibility
docs.text:
RECAP uses the call device's AHJ/CTIA combo headset connection (3.5mm TRRS). Phones, tablets and computers may provide it directly or through a compatible microphone-capable adapter; the app must actually route both call audio and the headset microphone through it.

Connection types to check:

  • iPhone (with 3.5mm jack or Lightning/USB-C to 3.5mm adapter)
  • Android phones with 3.5mm headphone jack
  • Laptops and computers with combo headset jack
  • Tablets with 3.5mm headphone jack
  • Any device using AHJ standard connector

Not compatible:

  • Devices without headphone jack and no adapter
  • Devices using OMTP standard (rare, mostly older European/Asian models)
  • Separate headphone + mic ports (not combo) — these won't pass both signals

How to check: Test the headset directly on CALL, using the same phone adapter and calling app. Hearing and being heard through the headset establishes that baseline; then repeat with RECAP and REC in the two-sided test.

No headphone jack on your phone? You need a Lightning or USB-C to 3.5mm adapter — and it has to be one that carries the microphone channel. Many cheap adapters do not, which leaves your phone using its own built-in microphone. Adapter guide (check the evidence for the exact model): https://recapmycalls.com/compatible-adapters-for-recap/

docs.title: Headset Compatibility
docs.text:
⚠️ The one rule that matters most: the microphone has to be on the headset cable.

RECAP is a passive splitter — it can only work with audio that physically travels through its cable. If your headset has no microphone on the cable, your voice never enters the chain: your call device uses its own built-in microphone instead. Your recording will be missing your side, and your callers may hear you as distant, since that microphone can be sitting on your desk while you wear the headset.

How to check: look along the cable for a boom arm, or a small inline blob partway down the wire (often with the volume buttons). That blob is the microphone. No boom and no blob means no microphone on the cable.

Requirements:

  • Wired, with a microphone on the cable — a 3.5mm TRRS plug (4-pole)
  • Must be compatible with YOUR call device
  • Reference headset: Apple 3.5mm EarPods. Other phone headsets must meet the same microphone and pinout requirements; a category name is not a test result.

A mic on the cable is the first requirement, and an inexpensive headset can meet it — the headset does not shape how your caller sounds in the recording, since that audio comes from the call itself. Headset quality still affects how you sound, though: a weak or noisy microphone shows up on your own channel. And a small number of TRRS headsets use a reversed pinout or an unusual connector and still misbehave — see Common incompatibilities below.

These cannot work with RECAP:

Headset type Why not What you'd see Listening-only earphones (3-pole TRS plug) No microphone on the cable. Common with music earphones and audiophile IEMs, which often ship with a mic-less cable. Call audio works, and recordings capture the caller but not you USB headsets Connect digitally. RECAP taps the analog 3.5mm signal, so a USB headset never passes through it. RECAP is bypassed entirely Lightning or USB-C EarPods Have their own converter built into the plug, so they connect straight to the phone and bypass RECAP. RECAP is bypassed entirely Bluetooth / wireless headsets Nothing travels down a cable for RECAP to tap. RECAP is bypassed entirely

How to test compatibility:

A physical microphone on the cable and a call where both people can hear each other do not establish that the wired mic is active: CALL may still use its built-in mic. Follow the canonical physical microphone-routing check and two-sided test, using the same adapter and calling app. Confirm the wired mic route before adding RECAP, then verify the complete recording path. These results apply to the tested configuration.

Common incompatibilities:

  • Old headsets using OMTP standard (mic/ground pins reversed)
  • Headsets designed for different phone brands
  • Damaged or worn-out headsets
  • PC gaming headsets (often use different connector types)

⚠️ Important: Distance of microphone boom to mouth affects volume. Keep mic 1-2 inches from corner of mouth.

docs.title: Computer Compatibility
docs.text:
REC needs a stereo microphone input, not just stereo headphone output. Computer age, port color and the word "stereo" in a product listing do not establish that its input captures two channels. A combo headset jack carries stereo headphone output plus a mono microphone input; it cannot directly capture S2's two recording channels. A headphone output cannot record at all.

Use the Audio Device Scanner to check the selected input's reported channel capability. It does not measure plug-in power, prove a signal is present, or certify the complete chain. Confirm capture with the two-sided test.

Input RECAP recording setup External stereo MIC input Use MIC mode and plug-in power where supported; record two channels Mono MIC / combo headset input Cannot preserve both S2 channels directly Line-only input Outside the supported MIC setup; not validated here Headphone/speaker output Output only, cannot capture audio

If the computer lacks the required input, use an interface that supplies an actual stereo microphone input, not merely stereo playback. See the compatible adapters guide and the exact model's manufacturer documentation.

docs.title: Recording Device Compatibility
docs.text:
Digital voice recorders and portable/field recorders are candidates when their external input meets these checks. A stereo built-in microphone does not prove that an external jack accepts stereo.

  • 3.5 mm TRS stereo external microphone input with two captured channels.
  • MIC mode, if the jack switches between mic and line; retain the supported plug-in-power setup, enabled where selectable.
  • Select the external input and stereo recording, preserving both channels. Disable mono mixing, noise reduction and automatic processing for the test.
  • Use the included TRS recording cable, not a TRRS headset cable.
  • Never connect RECAP to 48 V phantom power. A single balanced XLR/TRS input is not a stereo microphone input, even if it has three contacts.

Check the exact model's manufacturer manual, then make the two-sided test recording. A phone's Lightning/USB-C headphone adapter normally exposes a combo headset input, not this stereo recording input. Using a second mobile device as REC requires a stereo microphone interface supported by that device and recording app; a connector adapter alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Plug-in power and voltage: validation pending
docs.text:
Earlier versions of this manual said recorder bias powers S2 and specified a 2 V maximum. That explanation and limit were not adequately supported. Review of the archived S2 v40 fabrication artwork shows a passive resistor/capacitor circuit with a series coupling capacitor on each recording channel. This conflicts with the earlier DC-power explanation. Revision applicability and bench validation remain open; we have not established a validated S2 interface voltage range.

Keep the documented stereo MIC-mode / plug-in-power setup while validation is pending. A capacitor's 10 V component rating does not establish a 10 V safe interface limit, and this correction does not validate line-only inputs or higher voltages. Do not connect phantom power.

For example, the Zoom H1essential manual specifies a stereo mini input, 2 kΩ impedance and 2.5 V plug-in power. The H4essential manual specifies a stereo mini input, at least 2 kΩ and selectable plug-in power, without establishing its voltage. These are specification-based candidates, subject to the open S2 interface validation. No exact-model RECAP physical test or complete iPhone/Teams chain test has been established for these examples. They are not certified setups.

docs.title: What's NOT Compatible
docs.text:
❌ LINE IN ports

  • Outside the supported external stereo MIC setup; line-only operation is not validated here
  • Usually blue color or line icon
  • Found on: Older desktops, some Macs, stereo equipment

❌ +48V Phantom Power

  • Professional mixer equipment
  • Never connect RECAP to phantom power. It is different from microphone plug-in power.
  • See the pending voltage validation; no numerical S2 interface limit is established here.

⚠️ Mobile devices as recorder (requires USB adapter)

  • iPhones, iPads, Android phones/tablets have combo ports only
  • RECAP requires stereo MIC IN, which combo ports don't provide
  • Solution: USB audio adapter with stereo mic input, connected via USB-C or Lightning
  • Example: USB-C audio interface with 3.5mm stereo mic input

❌ Splitter cables

  • No supported configuration for using splitters
  • Splitters are for different purpose (sharing audio)

docs.title: The 5-Minute Diagnostic
docs.text:
Use this flowchart to diagnose any problem with your recording.

Run tests IN ORDER. Don't skip steps.

⚠️ Wrong page if your problem is the live call. This flowchart diagnoses what lands in your recording. If your callers say you sound muffled or distant while you're talking, none of these tests will help — you can pass all five and still have the problem. Go to Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant instead.

docs.title: Test 3B: Checking Device Settings (Critical!)
docs.text: After scanner shows STEREO, don't celebrate yet! Modern audio devices have "enhancement" features that can interfere with RECAP.

docs.title: How to Check Device Settings
docs.text:
1. On the scanner page, click on the device name (e.g., "Microphone (Realtek Audio)")
  2. The device card will expand to show detailed settings
  3. Look for these features and their status:

Interference Features (should be OFF):

  • Echo Cancellation - Designed to remove echo, but may suppress one channel thinking it's an echo
  • Noise Suppression - Filters background noise, but can kill quiet voices or merge channels
  • Auto Gain Control (AGC) - Automatically adjusts volume, but may apply different gain to each channel

Common problems when these are ON:

  • One-sided recording (only hear yourself OR only hear them)
  • Merged channels (both sides mixed into mono)
  • Inconsistent volume levels
  • Audio dropouts or distortion

docs.title: How to Fix Interference
docs.text:
Option 1: Via Audio Scanner (if supported)

  • Use the toggle switches in the expanded device view
  • Turn OFF Echo Cancellation, Noise Suppression, and Auto Gain Control
  • Adjust gain sliders to desired level (usually 80-100%)

Option 2: Via Operating System Settings

Windows:

  1. Right-click speaker icon → "Sounds"
  2. Go to "Recording" tab
  3. Select the device → "Properties"
  4. Enhancements tab → Check "Disable all enhancements" OR uncheck specific features
  5. Levels tab → Set microphone to 80-100%
  6. Click OK

Mac:

  1. System Preferences → Sound → Input
  2. Select the device
  3. Note: Mac has fewer audio processing options than Windows
  4. If issues persist, check the selected external input, gain and processing with the two-sided test before considering an interface change

docs.title: Using the VU Meters
docs.text:
While on the scanner page with device expanded:

  1. Make a short test call with REC capturing the connected external stereo input.
  2. Say a phrase into the headset mic while the other participant pauses; watch which channel responds.
  3. Have the other participant say a different phrase while you pause; the other channel should respond.
  4. One channel moving during one participant's phrase is expected. Both bars need not move together. Some crosstalk may appear; confirm each voice is captured mainly on its own channel by inspecting and playing back the separate channels.
  5. If a participant's phrase is missing, or both channels carry the same mix, check input selection, stereo/mono mode, headset/app routing and processing. The meter pattern is a clue, not a diagnosis of interference, adapter failure or unit condition. Follow the two-sided test.

docs.title: Test 3C: Baseline Stereo Test (Critical!)
docs.text:
Before troubleshooting RECAP further, verify your computer can record stereo audio at all.

Many customers have NEVER successfully recorded stereo audio on their computer before using RECAP. If the computer/software isn't configured correctly, RECAP won't work either.

docs.title: Why This Test Matters
docs.text:
What this checks: whether the same external recording input can capture two channels independently of the RECAP call chain. It does not establish the condition of the RECAP unit.

Common issues this catches: - RECAP plugged into a line-only input rather than the supported stereo MIC setup - Recording software defaulting to MONO mode - Wrong port selected in recording software - Computer genuinely lacks stereo capability (scanner false positive)

docs.title: How to Perform Baseline Test
docs.text:
You'll need: A verified two-channel stereo microphone connected to the same physical external input

Test procedure:

  1. Unplug RECAP temporarily
  2. Plug in a stereo microphone to the same port you were using for RECAP
  3. Open your recording software (Audacity, Sound Recorder, etc.)
  4. Set recording mode to STEREO (not mono!) - this is critical
  5. Test each channel separately, following the microphone manufacturer's channel-check instructions. Present a sound close to one capsule/input at a time, then the other, while watching separate left/right recording meters or waveforms. Each stimulus must produce a different left/right response.
  6. Inspect both channels and play them back separately. A stereo file containing the same signal duplicated into both channels is not a pass. If you cannot distinguish independent channel responses, the baseline remains unverified.

docs.title: What Qualifies as a Stereo Microphone?
docs.text:
Use a microphone whose manufacturer confirms two-channel stereo capture through that same external input. Stereo headphones can have a mono headset microphone; phone earbuds and gaming headsets do not establish a stereo recording baseline. A built-in or USB microphone tests a different input and cannot validate the jack RECAP uses.

Don't have a stereo mic? Continue to Test 4 and use the two-sided RECAP test. If it fails, contact support with the result; do not buy another microphone solely to complete this baseline.

docs.title: Interpreting Results
docs.text:
✅ Baseline test PASSED (independent left/right responses confirmed): - Your computer CAN record stereo - Your recording software is configured correctly - The tested input captured the two-channel stimulus; this does not measure its voltage or validate RECAP's electrical interface - Conclusion: The external input captured the baseline. Next isolate the complete RECAP call path; this result alone does not identify a cause. - Next step: Continue to Test 4

❌ Baseline test FAILED (stereo mic did NOT record): - The baseline did not capture stereo. Check the selected input, test microphone and recording mode before interpreting the RECAP test - Common causes: - Using LINE IN port instead of MIC IN port - Recording software set to MONO mode - Wrong input device selected in software - Gain set to 0% - Scanner incorrectly reported STEREO (actually MONO) - Next step: Fix computer setup BEFORE trying RECAP again

docs.title: How to Fix Failed Baseline
docs.text:
If baseline test failed, fix these issues:

Check port type: - Pink jack = MIC IN ✅ (correct) - Blue jack often indicates LINE IN; confirm the actual input specification - Green jack = Speaker/Headphone OUT ❌ (wrong)

Check recording software: - Audacity: Audio Setup → Recording Channels → 2 (Stereo) - Sound Recorder (Windows): Should auto-detect, but check input device selection - QuickTime (Mac): File → New Audio Recording → Click dropdown next to record button → Select stereo device

Check input device: - Recording software must select the correct device - Don't use "Default" - explicitly select the stereo-capable device - If using USB adapter, select "USB Audio Device" not "Realtek"

Check gain: - Windows: Sounds → Recording → Device → Properties → Levels → 80-100% - Mac: System Preferences → Sound → Input → Input volume slider to right

docs.title: When You Need It
docs.text:
Consider an interface only after checking the actual recording input:

  • A scanner MONO report is a clue: confirm the selected physical external input and capture mode first.
  • If that input is confirmed mono, or there is no supported external stereo MIC input, use another compatible stereo MIC input/interface.
  • A working headset pass-through with a failed recording does not by itself show an adapter is needed. Check routing, input selection, recording mode, gain and processing.
  • Computer brand or age alone does not establish input capability. Use the compatibility checklist and two-sided test.

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
RECAP outputs stereo audio (2 channels):

  • One channel = Your voice
  • Other channel = Their voice
  • ⚠️ Channel assignment (L/R) may vary depending on USB adapter

Your computer needs stereo input to record both channels.

A confirmed mono capture cannot preserve S2's two separate recording channels. A one-sided recording can also result from input selection, routing, cabling, gain or processing; it does not identify a cause on its own.

Neither a scanner channel count nor a one-sided recording establishes the condition of the RECAP unit. Use controlled tests to isolate the affected path.

docs.title: The Solution: A USB Stereo Mic Adapter
docs.text:
If the existing input lacks the required capability, an interface with a verified stereo microphone input can supply it. A USB connector or stereo headphone output alone does not establish that capability.

What it has to do — these are the criteria, not a brand:

  • ✅ Stereo microphone input (2 channels) — the one that matters most
  • ✅ Supplies bias voltage (plug-in power) to the mic input
  • ✅ Plug-and-play on your OS, no drivers

Which specific models we currently recommend, and where to buy them, is on the compatible adapters guide. That list is kept up to date as hardware and prices change — this manual deliberately doesn't name models, so the two can't drift apart.

docs.title: How to Use USB Adapter
docs.text:
Connections:

flowchart LR
    Phone[📱 Phone] --> RECAP[⚡ RECAP]
    RECAP --> Headset[🎧 Headset]
    RECAP -->|3.5mm cable| USBAdapter[🔌 USB Adapter<br/>MIC IN jack]
    USBAdapter -->|USB cable| Computer[💻 Computer<br/>USB port]

    style USBAdapter fill:#ffd43b,stroke:#f08c00

Setup steps:

  1. Plug USB adapter into computer's USB port
  2. Connect RECAP's output to USB adapter's MIC IN jack
  3. Computer will automatically recognize "USB Audio Device"
  4. In recording software, select "USB Audio Device" as input
  5. Test recording - should now capture both channels

That's it! The USB adapter gives your computer a true stereo microphone input.

docs.title: Checking Any Adapter Yourself
docs.text:
If the ones on the guide aren't available where you are, look for:

Required features:

  • Stereo microphone input (2 channels) - most important
  • Bias voltage for external microphones
  • Specifications mention "stereo mic input" or "2-channel input"

NOT compatible:

  • USB adapters with only LINE IN
  • USB adapters with only MONO mic input (1 channel)
  • Bluetooth adapters (too much latency for real-time)

docs.title: Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant
Problem: Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant
docs.text:
Symptom: People on the other end say your voice sounds muffled, distant, far away, or like you're on speakerphone — or they keep asking you to repeat yourself.

⚠️ This page is about the live call, not the recording. If your recording is silent, one-sided, or too quiet, you are on the wrong page — see No Audio Recorded or Low Volume & Noise. Those tests examine the recording output, and they cannot grade what your caller hears. (One exception: if your own voice is completely missing from a recording, check both the headset mic and the recording input; that symptom alone does not establish the cause. See only one side recorded.)

How to tell which one you have: if you are repeating what other people told you ("everybody says I sound muffled"), you are on the right page. If you are describing something you played back yourself, you want the recording pages above.

docs.title: Step 1: Get a measurement you can repeat
docs.text:
"Muffled" is a judgement call, and asking a caller to grade you gives a slightly different answer every time. Use your own voicemail instead — it travels the same microphone path your callers hear, and you can replay it as often as you like.

To reach your own voicemail: dialling your own number from your own phone usually drops you into your mailbox rather than your greeting. Instead, call your carrier's voicemail access number and use the "leave a message" option, or call a second phone you own and let it ring through to voicemail.

Then, at each rung below:

  1. Leave a short message — ten seconds is plenty, and say the same sentence every time
  2. Play it back through the same headset
  3. Note how it sounds compared with the previous rung

Read it as a comparison, not a verdict. Voicemail is compressed, so it always sounds a little duller than a live call — even on a perfectly healthy setup. Don't judge one recording against how a live call sounds. What matters is whether a rung sounds worse than the rung before it.

docs.title: Step 2: The three-rung ladder
docs.text:
Add exactly one link to the chain per rung, and leave a voicemail after each. Adding two at once tells you nothing about which one caused it.

⚠️ Rung 1 only counts if you physically unplug RECAP and make a new call. If you're answering from what you already know about your setup, you're answering rung 2. This is the single most common reason this goes in circles.

Rung What's connected If it sounds worse at this rung 1 Headset → phone. RECAP completely out of the chain. This baseline symptom occurs with RECAP absent; it does not explain any additional degradation when RECAP or the recording path is added. Check headset/app routing and call conditions. Check Cause 1: the headset microphone, then Cause 2: the adapter. 2 Headset → RECAP → phone. Nothing in RECAP's MIC jack. See Cause 3: connection order, and check the headset is in the pass-through jack rather than the MIC jack. 3 Headset → RECAP → phone, plus the recording cable in RECAP's MIC jack. Rebuild the whole chain and plug the phone in LAST — don't just add the cable to what's already connected, or you'll break the connection order and get a misleading result. The recording connection introduces the observed change; see Cause 4 checks without treating them as a verdict.

Sounds the same at every rung? No added degradation was observed in that comparison. Call quality, signal strength, the room or the other line may be involved; an unchanged comparison does not certify every part or exclude intermittent behavior. Try the same test on a different phone or in a different location. If callers still say you sound muffled on a chain that tests clean at all three rungs, contact support and say exactly that.

docs.title: Cause 1 (most common): no microphone on the headset cable
docs.text:
RECAP is a passive splitter. It can only pass along audio that physically travels through its cable. If your headset has no microphone on the cable, your voice never enters the chain — your call device uses its own built-in microphone instead. That microphone may be lying on your desk while you are wearing the headset, so you can come across as distant.

The confusing part: your phone does this with any mic-less headset, so swapping one mic-less headset for another changes nothing, and it starts to look like a device fault when it isn't.

How to check: look along the headset cable for a boom arm, or a small inline blob partway down the wire (often with the volume buttons). That blob is the microphone. No boom and no blob means no microphone on the cable.

These cannot work with RECAP:

Headset type Why not What you'd see Listening-only earphones (3-pole TRS plug) No microphone on the cable. Common with music earphones and audiophile IEMs, which often ship with a mic-less cable. Call audio works, and recordings capture the caller but not you USB headsets Connect digitally. RECAP taps the analog 3.5mm signal, so a USB headset never passes through it. RECAP is bypassed entirely Lightning or USB-C EarPods Have their own converter built into the plug, so they connect straight to the phone and bypass RECAP. RECAP is bypassed entirely Bluetooth / wireless headsets Nothing travels down a cable for RECAP to tap. RECAP is bypassed entirely

The fix: a wired 3.5mm headset with a microphone on the cable (a 4-pole TRRS plug). Apple's 3.5mm EarPods are a widely available known-good reference. See Headset Compatibility — a small number of TRRS headsets use a reversed pinout or an unusual connector and still misbehave, which is why a known-good headset is the fastest way to rule this out.

docs.title: Cause 2: the adapter doesn't carry the microphone channel
docs.text:
If your phone has no headphone jack, there is a Lightning or USB-C to 3.5mm adapter in your chain — and it is still there at rung 1, because rung 1 only removes RECAP. Many inexpensive adapters pass audio to your ears but don't carry the microphone channel back. The result is the same as Cause 1: the phone falls back to its own built-in microphone.

How to check: try a different adapter, ideally one from the tested list — https://recapmycalls.com/compatible-adapters-for-recap/ — and repeat the rung 1 voicemail.

docs.title: Cause 3: connection order
docs.text:
Your phone decides how to route audio at the instant something is plugged in. If the headset is not already in the chain when the phone sees the adapter, the phone can lock into the wrong routing mode and leave your microphone on the wrong path.

Connect in this order, every time:

  1. Headset into RECAP's headset jack
  2. Recording cable into RECAP's MIC jack (if you're recording)
  3. RECAP into the Lightning/USB-C adapter
  4. Adapter into the phone last

Full explanation and the iPhone reset path: Audio Routes to Speaker or One Ear with Lightning/USB-C Adapter.

docs.title: Cause 4: wrong jack, or the wrong recording cable
docs.text:
This one only shows up at rung 3 — fine without the recording cable, worse with it. That comparison localizes a change introduced when the recording connection is added; it does not establish the cause. A wrong jack or cable is one possibility. The unit, recorder/input loading, contact or grounding interaction also remains possible until isolated. Start with two visible checks:

  1. The recording cable is in RECAP's MIC jack, not the headset pass-through jack.
  2. The recording cable is the 3-pole (TRS) cable that ships in the box. Count the black bands on the plug: 2 bands = TRS (correct), 3 bands = TRRS (wrong). A 4-pole cable looks close enough to be missed, but it can ground on the wrong conductor — most often showing up as a unit that appears dead, or a recording missing your voice. If you swapped in your own cable, repeat with the boxed TRS cable as a controlled comparison; a changed result localizes that cable/connection combination rather than proving the unit's condition.

If the jacks and TRS cable are correct and rung 3 still degrades the call, note which recorder/input is connected and the comparison result, then contact support. Support can help isolate the recording path, including unit behavior and loading; this result alone does not justify buying another cable, adapter or recorder.

docs.title: Still worse at rung 1?
docs.text:
Rung 1 has RECAP completely out of the chain, so a symptom present there also occurs without RECAP. Check headset/adapter routing and call conditions; that baseline alone does not explain an additional change at rung 2 or 3. Work through Cause 1 and Cause 2 first.

If you've confirmed there's a microphone on the headset cable and tried a known-good adapter and rung 1 is still worse, contact support and tell us which rung number it first got worse at, your headset make and model, and which adapter is in the chain. That saves several rounds of back-and-forth.

docs.title: Problem: Low Volume or Faint Audio
docs.text:
Symptom: Recording is very quiet, have to turn volume way up to hear

⚠️ This is about your recording. If your callers say you sound faint, quiet, or distant during the call, that's a different signal path and none of the gain settings below will fix it — see Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant.

Solutions (try in order):

1. ⭐ MOST COMMON: Audio input gain too low

This fixes 90% of low volume issues!

  • Windows:
  • Right-click speaker icon in taskbar
  • Select "Recording devices"
  • Double-click "Microphone"
  • Go to "Levels" tab
  • Set "Microphone" slider to 100%

  • If there's "Microphone Boost" option, try +20dB

  • Mac:

  • System Preferences → Sound
  • Click "Input" tab
  • Drag "Input volume" slider all the way to the right

2. Headset microphone position

  • Boom mic should be 1-2 inches from corner of mouth
  • Not directly in front (causes breath noise)

3. Recording software input level

  • Many programs have their own gain slider
  • In Audacity: Input level slider at top (set to 0.8-1.0)

4. Phone call volume

  • During test call, increase phone volume with buttons
  • Affects how loud other person sounds in recording

5. Weak headset microphone

  • Some cheap headsets have poor quality
  • Try different headset (Apple EarPods are good reference)

docs.title: Problem: Audio Routes to Speaker or One Ear with Lightning/USB-C Adapter
docs.text:
Symptom: Audio plays through phone speaker instead of headset, or only one ear works — but only when using a Lightning or USB-C to 3.5mm adapter.

Cause: When you plug a Lightning or USB-C adapter into your phone, the phone immediately performs accessory detection. It decides whether the accessory is "Headphones," "Headset," or something else (like "Dock speaker"). If the adapter is plugged in without a headset already connected through RECAP, the phone may lock into the wrong audio routing mode.

This affects all modern phones: - iPhone (Lightning): Decides "Headphones" vs "Dock speaker" at plug-in - iPhone 15+ (USB-C): Same detection behavior - Android (USB-C): Per the Android spec, USB-C audio adapters don't present audio endpoints until a device is detected and its impedance is measured

Solution — connect in the right order:

  1. Plug your headset into RECAP's headset jack
  2. Plug the recording cable into RECAP's MIC jack (if using a computer)
  3. Plug RECAP into the Lightning/USB-C adapter
  4. Plug the adapter into your phone LAST

The full chain must be connected before the phone sees it.

If you already plugged in wrong order:

  1. Unplug the adapter from the phone
  2. Make sure headset is connected to RECAP
  3. Plug the adapter back in

iPhone reset (if it's still routing wrong): Settings → Sounds & Haptics → Headphone Safety → USB Accessories → "Forget All" — then reconnect.

If the order is right and it still misbehaves, check the adapter itself. Many inexpensive adapters don't carry the microphone channel at all, which leaves your phone using its own built-in microphone — a common reason callers say you sound distant. Tested adapters: https://recapmycalls.com/compatible-adapters-for-recap/

References:

  • Apple Support — Use Apple wired headphones
  • Android AOSP — USB-C audio adapter spec

docs.title: Problem: Can't Hear Call in Headset
docs.text:
Symptom: No audio in headset during call (but RECAP is connected)

Diagnostic:

  1. Test headset directly with phone (no RECAP)
  2. Does it work?
  3. NO → Headset is incompatible, get different one

  4. YES → Continue to #2

  5. Check connections

  6. RECAP firmly plugged into phone?
  7. Headset firmly plugged into RECAP?

  8. Try unplugging and reconnecting firmly

  9. Try different headset

  10. Confirms if it's headset compatibility issue

  11. If none of above work

  12. May be RECAP hardware defect
  13. Contact support with test results

docs.title: Problem: Static, Noise, or Interference
docs.text:
Common causes and solutions:

  1. Loose connections
  2. Ensure all plugs fully inserted

  3. Try unplugging and reconnecting firmly

  4. Dirty or damaged connectors

  5. Use compressed air to clean jacks

  6. Look for bent pins

  7. Electrical interference

  8. Move RECAP away from power adapters, monitors

  9. Don't let cables run parallel to power cords

  10. Microphone gain too high (causing distortion)

  11. Lower gain to 70-80%

  12. Look for clipping in waveform (flattened peaks)

  13. Poor quality headset

  14. Some cheap headsets have noisy electronics
  15. Try different headset

docs.title: Problem: Left and Right Channels Are Swapped
docs.text:
Symptom: Your voice is on the right channel and the caller is on the left (or vice versa from what you expected)

This is normal — not a defect. RECAP's hardware outputs your voice on one channel and the caller's voice on the other, but which is "left" and which is "right" depends on your recording device. USB audio adapters, voice recorders, and some computer sound cards interpret the Tip and Ring pins differently, which can swap the channels.

How to verify:

  1. Record a short test call
  2. Open the recording in Audacity
  3. Split Stereo to Mono (track dropdown → Split Stereo to Mono)
  4. Play each track — note which is you and which is the caller
  5. Label them for future reference

This only matters if you need to edit channels independently. If you just play back the full recording, you'll hear both voices regardless of which channel they're on.

If you need to swap channels in Audacity:

  1. Split Stereo to Mono
  2. Drag one track above/below the other to reorder
  3. Track dropdown → Make Stereo Track

docs.title: Problem: Not Working on Mac
docs.text:
Most Macs have MONO-only or LINE IN ports

Diagnostic:

  1. Run device scanner: https://recapmycalls.com/audio/
  2. Most Macs show MONO only → USB adapter needed

Mac audio port types:

  • Combo port (one port for headphones + mic): Usually MONO only
  • Separate input jack: Often LINE IN, not MIC IN (incompatible)

Solution: a USB stereo mic adapter — how to use it · which ones

docs.title: Problem: No Audio Recorded
docs.text:
Symptom: Recording file is silent or shows flat waveform

Is this about your recording, or about the live call? Everything on this page is about what lands in the recording. If your problem is that callers say you sound muffled or distant while you're talking, that's a different signal path with different tests — see Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant.

Work through the diagnostic flowchart. These are checks, not a diagnosis from silence alone:

  1. Check the selected input and channel mode
  2. Run scanner: https://recapmycalls.com/audio/

  3. Confirm the actual external input and capture mode with the two-sided test. Consider an interface only if that input is confirmed insufficient; see input checks.

  4. Audio input gain too low/muted

  5. Windows: Right-click speaker icon → Recording devices → Microphone → Properties → Levels → Set to 100%
  6. Mac: System Preferences → Sound → Input → Drag slider all the way right

  7. Speak into headset - do you see level meter moving?

  8. Headset incompatible with phone

  9. Test headset directly with phone (no RECAP)

  10. Old headsets from drawers often don't work

  11. Connected to LINE IN instead of MIC IN

  12. Use the supported external stereo MIC mode, with plug-in power where supported; line-only operation is not validated

  13. Look for port with microphone icon or pink color

  14. Wrong input device selected in software

  15. Check recording software settings
  16. Select "RECAP" or "External Microphone"

docs.title: Problem: Only Hear in One Ear (Headset)
docs.text:
Symptom: During a call with RECAP connected, you only hear the caller in one ear of your headset.

This is NOT the stereo split. The stereo split only applies to the recording output (the cable going to your computer). The headset pass-through is transparent — it forwards your phone's audio to your headset untouched, exactly like plugging the headset directly into your phone. You should hear in both ears. See How RECAP Works for details.

If you only hear in one ear, check these:

  1. Headset plugged into wrong jack
  2. RECAP has two output jacks: the headset pass-through and the MIC recording output
  3. If your headset is in the MIC jack, you'll hear the stereo split (one side per ear) instead of normal call audio

  4. Move the headset to the pass-through jack

  5. Cable not fully seated

  6. Push the headset plug firmly into RECAP until it clicks
  7. Do the same for the phone-to-RECAP connection

  8. A partial insert can drop a channel

  9. Headset problem

  10. Test the headset directly in your phone (no RECAP)

  11. If it's still one ear, the headset is the issue

  12. Phone adapter issue

  13. If using a Lightning or USB-C to 3.5mm adapter, try a different one
  14. Some cheap adapters don't pass all channels correctly
  15. Tested adapters: https://recapmycalls.com/compatible-adapters-for-recap/

docs.title: Problem: Recording Only Has Audio on One Side
docs.text:
Symptom: You open your recording and only one channel has audio — the other is silent or very quiet.

If the caller is on the recording but your own voice is missing, check the recording input and the headset microphone path. This symptom alone does not identify a fault. Earlier guidance said recorder bias powers S2 and carries your voice; that mechanism is not supported by the reviewed v40 artwork. See the correction and pending validation. Keep these supported setup checks:

  • The recorder input is a stereo MIC input (not LINE IN) that supplies plug-in power. Your recorder's manual will say; see Recording Device Compatibility.
  • Your headset has a microphone on its cable. Without one, your phone uses its own mic and your voice never reaches RECAP. See Cause 1.
  • If your phone uses a Lightning or USB-C adapter, you connect the phone last. See connection order.

Also use the two-sided test to confirm actual external-input capture. On a computer, check the items below.

This is about the recording output, not headset playback. Check:

  1. Check the selected input and channel mode
  2. Many computers have mono microphone inputs; check the exact selected input rather than assuming from the brand
  3. A mono input can only capture one of RECAP's two channels
  4. Run the Audio Device Scanner to check

  5. The scan alone does not identify the cause. Use the two-sided test, and consider another input/interface only if the external input is confirmed unable to capture stereo.

  6. Echo cancellation or noise suppression enabled

  7. These features can merge or suppress one channel
  8. Run the scanner, expand your device, and disable Echo Cancellation and Noise Suppression

  9. See Device Scanner guide for details

  10. USB adapter swapping channels

  11. Some USB adapters reverse left and right
  12. Not a problem — just note which channel is you and which is the caller

docs.title: What RECAP Does
docs.text:
RECAP is a hardware audio converter. It sits between your phone and your headset, and it does two things at once:

  1. Passes call audio through to your headset — so you can talk normally, as if RECAP wasn't there.
  2. Sends a separate recording output to your computer — this is where both sides of the conversation are captured for recording.

These are two independent outputs. They carry different signals. Understanding this distinction is key to troubleshooting any audio issue.

Audio flow:

flowchart LR
    Phone[📱 YOUR PHONE<br/><br/>Phone call audio]
    RECAP[⚡ RECAP S2<br/><br/>Converts to stereo mic:<br/>Channel 1 = Your voice<br/>Channel 2 = Their voice]
    Headset[🎧 HEADSET<br/><br/>You hear call<br/>in real-time]
    Computer[💻 COMPUTER<br/><br/>Records stereo input<br/>Saves both sides]

    Phone -->|Headset audio| RECAP
    RECAP -->|Pass-through| Headset
    RECAP -->|Stereo microphone| Computer

    style Phone fill:#e7f5ff,stroke:#339af0
    style RECAP fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#f08c00
    style Headset fill:#d3f9d8,stroke:#2f9e44
    style Computer fill:#e7f5ff,stroke:#339af0

docs.title: Two Outputs, Two Different Signals
docs.text: This is the most important thing to understand about RECAP. It has two outputs and they work completely differently:

docs.title: Output 1: Pass-Through (Headset Jack)
docs.text:
The pass-through sends your phone's call audio straight to your headset. RECAP does not modify, split, or process this signal in any way. It is identical to plugging your headset directly into your phone.

  • You hear the caller in both ears, same as without RECAP
  • The caller hears you through the headset mic, same as without RECAP
  • The audio is mono (same sound in left and right ear) — this is normal for phone calls
  • If you unplugged the recording cable and never connected a computer, the pass-through would still work exactly the same

This assumes your headset has a microphone on the cable. If it doesn't, your call device uses its own built-in microphone instead — so your caller hears you from wherever the phone is sitting, which can make you sound distant. If people tell you that you sound muffled, start here: Callers Say I Sound Muffled or Distant.

Example: You're on a call with a client. You hear their voice in both ears of your headset, they hear your voice through the headset mic. You talk normally. From a call quality perspective, nothing has changed — RECAP is invisible.

If you only hear in one ear through the headset pass-through, that is not the recording split. Compare the direct-headset baseline and complete chain to isolate the path; see headset troubleshooting.

⚠️ If using a Lightning or USB-C adapter: Always connect the headset to RECAP first, then plug into the phone last. Your phone performs accessory detection at plug-in — if the headset isn't already in the chain, audio may route incorrectly. See Connection Order troubleshooting.

docs.title: Output 2: Recording Output (MIC Jack)
docs.text:
This is the separate cable that goes from RECAP to your computer (or voice recorder). This output is where RECAP does its real work — it captures both sides of the conversation and splits them into a stereo signal:

  • One channel = your voice (picked up from the headset mic)
  • The other channel = the caller's voice (picked up from the phone's audio)

Which one your recording shows as left and which as right depends on your recording device. Some devices swap them, which is normal. If it matters to you, check with a short test recording (Channel Swap).

This stereo split is intentional. It's the whole point of RECAP — it gives you clean, separated audio that you can edit, transcribe, or process independently.

Example: You record a 30-minute interview. When you open the recording in Audacity or any audio editor, you see two channels. One channel is you, the other is the interviewee. You can adjust volume on each independently, remove background noise from one side without affecting the other, or export just the caller's audio.

⚠️ The stereo split only exists on the recording output. It has nothing to do with what you hear in your headset during the call.

docs.title: Setup and two-sided test
docs.text:
Check the compatibility checklist first. CALL is the phone/device running the call; REC is the separate recorder.

  1. Test the wired TRRS headset directly on CALL with the same phone adapter and calling app. Confirm you hear the other person and they hear the headset mic. Move CALL away from your mouth and gently rub the headset's microphone housing while your test partner listens; compare with a gentle rub near CALL's built-in mic. The headset-mic sound should be prominent. If only the phone-mic sound is prominent, the wired mic route has not passed. Check the app's input/output route and repeat; Bluetooth, the phone speaker or built-in mic bypasses the intended wired path. An app permission alone does not prove routing.
  2. Disconnect from CALL. Connect the headset to RECAP's HEADSET pass-through, and the included 3-pole TRS recording cable from RECAP's MIC/recording output to REC's external stereo mic input. Connect RECAP to the phone adapter if needed, then connect the CALL phone last. See connection order.
  3. On REC, select that physical external input, MIC mode where selectable, plug-in power enabled where supported, and stereo/two-channel recording. Start with processing/mono mixing off. Follow the recorder's manual for controls.
  4. Record a short call (about 20–30 seconds). Say a phrase while the other person pauses, then have them say a different phrase while you pause. Keep the call audible only in the headset, so REC's built-in mic cannot pick up speaker audio.
  5. Stop and play back both recorded channels. Confirm both voices are audible at useful levels and each appears on its own channel. Note which side is yours; device/software channel labels can differ. Your voice alone does not prove the RECAP path is selected. A stereo setting alone does not prove two-sided capture.

Repeat when changing the phone, adapter, headset, recorder or calling app. For missing recording audio use No Audio Recorded; for what the caller hears use live-call troubleshooting. If the documented setup still fails, contact support with the symptom and test result; the failure alone does not establish which part is at fault.

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text:
Connection Interface Phone plug / headset pass-through 3.5 mm TRRS, AHJ/CTIA headset path Recording output (MIC jack) 3.5 mm TRS: Tip carries phone/caller audio, Ring carries headset-mic audio, Sleeve is common ground on reviewed v40 artwork Recorder setup External stereo MIC input, MIC mode and plug-in power where supported

Both recording paths appear AC-coupled in the archived v40 artwork. Earlier bias-power, impedance and voltage statements did not establish a validated interface specification; see the corrected requirements and pending validation. No batteries are required. Do not infer a safe interface voltage from a component rating, or use 48 V phantom power. Use the two-sided test to establish the channel assignment in your actual recording.

docs.title: Windows Software
docs.text:
Built-in: Sound Recorder

  • Pros: Already installed, simple one-button operation
  • Cons: Very basic, no editing features, saves to WMA format
  • Best for: Quick recordings, beginners

Recommended: Audacity (Free)

  • Download: https://www.audacityteam.org
  • Pros:
  • Free and open source
  • Shows stereo waveform (verify both channels recording)
  • Edit, trim, noise removal
  • Export to MP3, WAV, OGG
  • Works on Windows, Mac, Linux
  • Cons: Slightly more complex than Sound Recorder
  • Best for: Anyone wanting to edit or keep recordings long-term

How to use Audacity:

  1. Open Audacity
  2. Check input device at top: Should say "Microphone" or "RECAP"
  3. Click red record button
  4. Make your call
  5. Click yellow stop button
  6. File → Export → Export as MP3 (or WAV for best quality)

docs.title: Mac Software
docs.text:
Built-in: QuickTime Player

  • Pros: Already installed, simple interface
  • Cons: Basic features, saves to M4A format
  • Best for: Quick recordings

Recommended: Audacity (Free)

  • Same as Windows version (see above)
  • Download: https://www.audacityteam.org

docs.title: Recording Tips
docs.text:
Before recording:

  • Close other apps that use microphone (Zoom, Skype, etc.)
  • Check input levels (speak and watch meter)
  • Make a 10-second test recording first

During recording:

  • Keep headset mic 1-2 inches from corner of mouth
  • Don't touch RECAP device (can cause handling noise)
  • Monitor input levels if software shows them
  • Avoid loud background noise

After recording:

  • Listen to first 30 seconds before ending call
  • If one-sided or no audio, stop and troubleshoot immediately
  • Save in WAV format for highest quality (can convert to MP3 later)
  • Backup important recordings to cloud storage

File formats:

  • WAV: Uncompressed, best quality, large files (10MB per minute)
  • MP3: Compressed, good quality, small files (1MB per minute)
  • Recommendation: Record as WAV, convert to MP3 for sharing
